title: Old Timers' Room
subtitle: Historic Photographs & Traditions Since 1881
transcript: You have entered the Old Timers' Room of our museum. The photographs displayed here date back as far as 1881, when Deming was founded. In the early days of the railroad, the Santa Fe and the Southern Pacific railroads drove a silver spike just outside Deming to complete the second transcontinental railroad line. Steam locomotives could only travel 60 miles before they needed to refill their water tanks. Deming is 60 miles from Las Cruces; Lordsburg is 60 miles from Deming; and Silver City is 60 miles from Deming. Deming served as a water stop for those early railroad locomotives. Deming sprung up very quickly once the water stop was established. Sometime around 1900, some of the Deming businessmen started an annual tradition of having a lavish dinner party. They called themselves "The Old Timers". They had a growing collection of photographs that they would display in the windows of Mahoney's Hardware Store. That photograph collection is now on display in this room. There is also a list of the Old Timer's Association Presidents for the last 113 years. The wrought iron photo racks were built sometime in the early 1980s by Harold Measday. To this day, the Deming Old Timers meet every October with class reunions, a banquet and a dance. The Old Timer's celebration is the longest continuing celebration in the state of New Mexico. Of particular interest in the wrought iron photographs are: The Deming Harvey House Holy Cross Sanitarium Other notable photos in this room are: Framed picture of the big fire dated July 11, 1918 Deming High School class of 1932 yearbook Picture of Paul and Alma Feil, local doctor 1918 diploma of Frances Isabel Phillips Faded picture labelled "1902 picture of Horse & Buggy Days" Herman Perez age 112 in 1928 Artist's rendition of Deming in 1898 with a view looking south on Gold Street and the railroad station
highlights: 1881 Founding & 60-Mile Water Stop
Mahoney's Hardware Photos & Measday Racks
113-Year Old Timers' Reunion (NM's Longest Celebration)
Harvey House, 1918 Fire & Herman Perez (Age 112)

title: Mimbres Pottery & Prehistoric Culture
subtitle: Masterpieces of 950–1200 A.D. & Mogollon Heritage
transcript: About 5,000 Mimbres Indians lived along the Mimbres River and occupied the Deming, Silver City and Lordsburg area (Luna, Grant and Hidalgo counties) from 950 to 1200 A.D. It is thought they left the valley because the population had outgrown the resources. Perhaps they went to Mexico and joined tribes there. Perhaps they went north and scattered among the Anasazi pueblos of New Mexico and Arizona. Fortunately, they buried pottery with their dead under the floor of their homes. From digging archaeologists believe the Mimbres were small, had a life expectancy of 40 to 50 years and were a religious, agricultural people. Pots depict wedding ceremonies, christenings, babies carried on cradle boards, children playing and grandfather telling stories. One picture shows an old man with a cane and his hand on his back. Their pottery gives us ideas of their dress, hair styles, weapons and show their activities – hunting, snaring birds, ceremonial dancing, gambling, etc. The hole in the bottom of burial pottery was thought to have been put there to release the spirit of the bowl. The ceremonial "killing" of the pottery took place at the grave since the knocked-out pieces were found in the graves along with the killed vessel. Often the bowl was placed over the head of the deceased. Mimbres pottery was black on white and occasionally red on white. Painted with yucca leaf chewed into a brush, paints made from minerals on the earth. Designs were geometric and naturalistic (animals, humans, etc.). J.W. Fewkes, author, says "no Southwestern pottery, ancient or modern, surpasses that of the Mimbres; and its naturalistic figures are unexcelled in any pottery from prehistoric America. This superiority lies in the figures of the men and animals and in the geometric design." The Mimbres Indians position was unique as it was one of busiest places on the American continent as it was the only low-land route from the Atlantic to the Pacific Oceans, no navigation of mountains. This was a major factor in why the south intercontinental route of the railroad was placed here as well as the building of Interstate I-10.
highlights: 950–1200 A.D. Mimbres Mogollon Culture
World-Famous Black-on-White Painted Bowls
Ceremonial 'Kill Hole' Spirit Rituals
Chewed Yucca Leaf & Mineral Pigment Artistry
Historic Transcontinental Lowland Route

title: Building History
subtitle: Historic 1916 National Guard Armory & Architecture
transcript: Ground broke on this armory in 1915 — and just two months after Pancho Villa's infamous raid on nearby Columbus, New Mexico, in March 1916, construction was complete. It holds a special distinction: the first armory built in New Mexico after statehood in 1912, and today, it's the oldest armory still standing in the state. Over the decades, the building has worn many hats. It served as a community social hub, then transformed into a bustling USO activity center during World War II, offering troops a place to relax and connect. In 1977, the Luna County Historical Society saw its potential and purchased the armory for $11,500, turning it into a museum. The spark that set everything in motion? A single donated item — Deming's first electric washing machine — which arrived at the museum's original home, a modest little house with no room to spare. That one washing machine changed everything. It set off a chain of expansion that transformed a cramped house into the sprawling museum you can explore today: 25,000 square feet, 47 exhibits, two stories, and more than 85,000 items on display. The Historical Society now spans three buildings — the Museum, the Archives, and the Custom House, which is available for party rentals. Don't miss the Gift Shop on your way out, stocked with mementos and information on the Mimbres Indians, military history, and other Southwest treasures. Admission is free, but donations are always appreciated.
highlights: 1916 National Guard Armory Building
National Register of Historic Places
Exposed Timber Roof Trusses & Brickwork
Luna County Historical Society Heritage

title: Military Room
subtitle: Honoring Service, Bataan, WWII Airfield & Frontier Forts
transcript: Welcome to the Military Room. Along the left wall are photographs of Luna County residents who served in the various branches of our Armed Forces, and the cabinets around you hold insignia, uniforms, mementos, and challenge coins donated and loaned by local families. Look for the faded black-and-white photo of the 200th and 515th Coast Artillery — the New Mexico servicemen who would later take part in the Bataan Death March. A full exhibit on the march is located near the museum's entrance. World War II In the next room, you'll find uniforms, insignia, and mementos donated and loaned by WWII veterans and their families, along with several scale models of the ships and planes of the era. At the center of the room, a plexiglass case holds a Norden Mark XV Bombsight — the same model installed and tested in the B-17s that trained right here at the Deming Army Airfield. Beginning in March 1943, a new class of 150 to 200 bombardier students graduated every three weeks, and by the war's end nearly 8,000 bombardiers had trained in Deming. The Norden was considered revolutionary: for the first time, a mechanical computer was paired with an autopilot to promise real gains in bombing accuracy. Deming's airmen spent the rest of the war chasing that promise — and by the time the fighting ended, it still hadn't quite been kept. Fort Cummings Room This room is devoted to Fort Cummings, the first walled fort in the New Mexico Territory, garrisoned by the U.S. Cavalry from October 1863 until its abandonment in 1873. You can still trace the outline of its walls on the southeast side of Cooke's Peak, just west of Highway 26. For years, the fort was a regular stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail route. The cases here feature the uniforms, insignia, and artwork of the 9th and 10th Cavalry Regiments — the famed "Buffalo Soldiers." Camp Cody During World War I, Deming hosted one of several training camps built across the Southwest to take advantage of its sunshine and mild winters. Camp Cody — named for William "Buffalo Bill" Cody of Wild West Show fame — trained National Guard units from North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Minnesota, and Iowa. The camp opened on July 16, 1916, and closed in early 1919, not long after the Armistice of November 11, 1918, brought the war to an end. Many of its barracks, buildings, and mess halls were sold off afterward and are scattered throughout Luna County today. The camp hospital had a second life of its own: the Sisters of the Holy Cross later purchased it and ran it as a tuberculosis sanitarium through the 1920s and '30s. Pancho Villa Raid On March 9, 1916, Pancho Villa crossed into the United States and raided Columbus, New Mexico, killing several people. The Deming unit of the National Guard — whose flag is on display here — was dispatched immediately to Camp Furlong in Columbus. General John J. "Black Jack" Pershing then led a military expedition into Mexico in pursuit of Villa. It was a campaign of firsts: the first time cavalry forces used motorized trucks and motorcycles, and the first time the Army used its new Aero Squadron for aerial observation and scouting. A young George Patton took part as well, and it was here that he began developing the ideas that would shape his later strategy for tank warfare. The machine gun on display defended Columbus during the raid; it was buried for safekeeping, rediscovered in the 1960s, and brought here for display.
highlights: 200th & 515th Coast Artillery Bataan Tribute
Deming Army Airfield Norden Bombsight & B-17s
Fort Cummings & Buffalo Soldiers (9th/10th Cavalry)
Camp Cody WWI Camp & Holy Cross Sanitarium
March 9, 1916 Columbus Raid Defense Machine Gun

title: Bataan Death March Display
subtitle: 200th & 515th Coast Artillery Anti-Aircraft Heroes
transcript: This case is dedicated to the 200th & 515th Coast Artillery Anti-Aircraft Corps. Between April 9 and April 17, 1942, the Imperial Japanese Army forced roughly 75,000 American and Filipino prisoners of war on a 65-mile march from Mariveles to Camp O'Donnell on the Bataan Peninsula. The prisoners received almost no food or water, and thousands did not survive. They endured beatings, torture, and killings for even the smallest infractions — a man who asked for water might be shot on the spot. Some were forced to strip naked or sit within sight of fresh, cool water they could not touch. Trucks ran over those who collapsed from exhaustion, and "cleanup crews" killed prisoners too weak to continue, though other trucks did stop to carry some of the fallen onward. Men were beaten or stabbed with bayonets without warning. Estimates vary, but as many as 8,000 Filipino and 650 American soldiers died before ever reaching the camp. The march struck close to home in Deming: many of the American soldiers captured at Bataan came from New Mexico. The 200th & 515th Coast Artillery units numbered 1,816 men. 829 died in battle, in captivity, or shortly after liberation; 987 survived. By March 2017, only four of those veterans were still living. Since 1989, the Bataan Memorial Death March — a marathon-length, 26.2-mile march and run — has been held each spring at White Sands Missile Range in their memory. The cabinets around you hold newspaper articles and photographs donated by Deming-area POWs and their families. The large, framed plaque in the right-hand cabinet lists 83 Luna County residents who served in the 200th & 515th Coast Artillery Anti-Aircraft Corps; thirty of them were killed in action. Nearby is a shadow box donated by the family of Lee Gardner.
highlights: 200th & 515th Coast Artillery Anti-Aircraft Corps
April 1942 65-Mile Bataan Death March
83 Luna County Servicemen Plaque & 30 KIA
Deming POW Personal Letters, Photos & Shadowboxes
Annual Bataan Memorial Death March (White Sands)

title: Doll & Toy Room
subtitle: Auburn Rubber, Historic Dolls & Childhood Memories
transcript: The doll and toy room is unique as we have toys made from the pioneers settling in Luna County and from Auburn Rubber the largest producer of rubber and vinyl toys in American and probably the world. They moved their molds from Auburn, Indiana to Deming in 1959–1960 timeframe. We have a doll from the Pancho Villa Raid of March 9, 1916. The doll belonged to the daughter of the telephone operator who called in the raid. Glass shards rained on the daughter's head as bullets broke the window above the area where she was sleeping. We have a Japanese doll from the ashes of Hiroshima. The hair is real from a Japanese woman. An American soldier picked the doll from a pile of rubbish and later donated it to our museum. A walk through this room will bring back childhood memories of toys you may have likely played with as a child. This room and the adjoining Old Timers' Room you just walked through were originally a small-caliber indoor shooting range used by the soldiers stationed here. During World War II, when this building served as a USO, these two rooms were converted to a bowling alley.
highlights: Auburn Rubber Toys (Deming 1959–1960)
1916 Pancho Villa Raid Survivor Doll
Hiroshima Japanese Doll Artifact
Armory Shooting Range & WWII USO Bowling Alley

title: Transportation Annex
subtitle: Harvey House, 1904 REO, Fire Truck & Railroad History
transcript: Transportation has shaped life in Deming and throughout the Southwest for generations. From wagons and railroads to automobiles and modern highways, each advancement changed how people traveled, worked, traded and stayed connected, On March 18, 1881, the Santa Fe and Southern Pacific Railroad met to create the southern transcontinental railroad line. A silver spike was driven to join the east/west railroad lines. Charles Crocker was one of the four railroad barons and Deming is named after his wife – Mary Deming-Crocker. We have a display of many railroad items and what a station would have. Deming had one of the grandest Harvey Houses in the Southwest with linen tablecloths, with gourmet meals served on silver and china. The waitresses were called Harvey Girls and were single, young women of "good character". By 1891 there were 15 Harvey Houses from Kansas to the southwest. This was the first restaurant chain in America. Unfortunately, our Harvey House was burnt to the ground in a grand fire. The Harvey House display has the original paint and lumber from the original. The Santa Fe employees in Deming donated the items so the museum Harvey House would look authentic. The train station does exist. The Deming sign is from the station. The station is located on north Country Club Road and is used for speaking engagements and offices. Our vehicle display is of interest — the first fire truck of Deming. Go ahead, ring the bell and turn the handle for the siren! The children (big and small) love it. The 1904 REO is the first vehicle owned by a Deming resident. We are fortunate to have other transportation vehicles. And yes, even though we are in a very flat area we do have two soap-box derby cars. The races were held in El Paso. That was quite a way to travel to race those cars. Explore the journey. The Transportation exhibit invites visitors to step into the past to explore how movement changed communities over time. Whether you are into local history, engineering, trains, classic vehicles or how locals travelled, this exhibit offers a unique look into how the southwest developed.
highlights: 1881 Silver Spike & Mary Deming-Crocker
Historic Harvey House & Harvey Girls Display
Original Deming Train Station Sign & Railroad Gear
Deming's First Volunteer Fire Truck with Working Bell & Siren
1904 REO Automobile & Historic Soap Box Derby Racers

title: Medical Room
subtitle: Historic Healthcare, 1940s/50s Iron Lungs & Deming Sanitaria
transcript: This room may be difficult for some visitors, as it illustrates the medical practices and equipment in everyday use. The items were donated by the doctors and the hospitals that served Deming from the 1930's through the 1950's. Among the most striking pieces are two iron lungs – an adult version and an infant/child – that were used during the polio epidemics of 1949 and 1952. The Women's Hospital donated them to the Deming Memorial Hospital and funds were raised by the Deming Rotary Club to purchase and then donate them to the Museum. You'll also find a wooden birth chair from Spain, along with artifacts from hospitals and clinics throughout the Deming area, including the Women's Hospital, Faywood Hot Springs, the Camp Cody Red Cross Building and Infirmary, and Holy Cross Hospital, which operated for many years as a tuberculosis sanitarium. The nun doll on display was donated by the Holy Cross Order of South Bend, Indiana, along with a research paper detailing the order's history establishing and running the Holy Cross Sanitarium in Deming. Medicine has come a long way since these tools were in daily use.
highlights: 1949 & 1952 Polio Epidemic Adult & Infant Iron Lungs
Deming Rotary Club & Women's Hospital Donations
Antique Spanish Wooden Birthing Chair
Camp Cody Red Cross Infirmary & Faywood Hot Springs
Holy Cross Tuberculosis Sanitarium & Sister Doll

title: Western Area
subtitle: Ranching Life, Diamond A Chuckwagon & Ruebush Saddlery
transcript: Deming was founded as a railroad town that soon expanded into a booming agriculture hub for farming and ranching. Ranchers would spend days, even weeks riding the range in all elements of our environment, tending to their herds. To get the job of branding and gathering of cattle for shipping on the railroad, packing the right equipment and supplies were crucial. The chuck wagon on display is from the Diamond A Ranch located in Hachita, New Mexico and is made from multiple parts of other wagons. Many meals were served from this wagon to very hungry men and boys. Cast iron pans, Dutch ovens, a boiling pot and water barrel and branding irons were carefully loaded aboard. Supplies consisting of flour, cornmeal, pinto beans, green coffee beans, salt pork, beef jerky and bacon were the primary staples on the long cattle drive. This chuck wagon was last used on a drive in 1972. One of the most important parts of a rancher's comfort is his saddle. On display are saddles donated from various local ranching families. The majority of these were made locally in the early 1930s and 1940s by Ruebush Saddlery. The store was located on Silver Street until the late 1970s. The cowboy hats are donated by the families and individual cowboys. It was said the creasing, the brim and the tilt of the hat were distinctive and that in a distance another cowboy knew who person was by these markers.
highlights: Historic Diamond A Ranch Chuckwagon (Hachita, NM)
Last Used on a Cattle Drive in 1972
Deming's Historic Ruebush Saddlery (Silver Street)
Luna County Registered Branding Irons & Tack
Donated Southwestern Cowboy Hats & Chuckwagon Gear

title: Quilt & Lace Room
subtitle: Hand-Stitched Heritage, 1820s Spreads & Lottie Deno Lace
transcript: European settlers — the Dutch and English among them — brought the tradition of quilting to America in the 17th century. Early quilts were practical creations, often pieced together from fabric scraps and recycled clothing. Over time, quilting bees became cherished social gatherings, giving women a chance to work side by side, trade stories, and strengthen the bonds of their community. The oldest quilt in this room is a hand-woven spread dating to around 1820, donated in memory of Bessie Gomer May, the woman largely responsible for this museum's existence. Look closely and you'll also find fine examples of tatting lace, made from an intricate series of knots and loops. One piece of particular interest is an altar cloth made by Lottie "Deno" Thurman — known formally as Mrs. Frank Thurman. Lottie led a colorful life in Deming and was renowned as a remarkably shrewd gambler; her reputation was so notable that she's said to have inspired the character of Miss Kitty on the television series Gunsmoke. Several books on Lottie Deno's life are available online, or ask about them in our Gift Store.
highlights: 17th-Century Quilting Traditions & Quilting Bees
Circa 1820 Hand-Woven Spread (Bessie Gomer May Memorial)
Intricate Tatting Lace Knots & Loops
Lottie 'Deno' Thurman Handcrafted Altar Cloth
Inspiration for Miss Kitty of TV's Gunsmoke

title: Main Street Display
subtitle: Historic Storefronts, 1890s Hearse & The Deming Headlight
transcript: Upon this location's opening, the museum started to receive so many donations that it ran out of room and discussions were held to add additions. One such discussion was to recreate a store front exhibit of Deming. What you see first are horse drawn carriages. A hearse donated by Baca Funeral Home last used in the 90s; buggies most likely used for going to church and courting your special someone; a sleigh even though Deming only receives an average of nine inches of total precipitation per year; and various wagons used by families, farmers, and ranchers. To the right of the hearse is Deming's first traffic light and an old gas pump. Great additions! The recreated shops illustrate what items were available and applicable to the store. The Mahoney Hardware has the washing machine that is the reason this museum is what you see now. Dental office, beauty salon, dress shop, post office, the livery stable, funeral parlor with an old casket and clothing for burial purposes, barber shop and so much more. Several store fronts have original signs. Look closely at each store front to absorb the era of the time. The Deming Headlight is of particular interest as it is considered the oldest continuously published newspaper in the state even though it is twice a week now. A look in the window one will see an old typewriter and an over-engineered pencil sharpener We have their old, old, printing press. A big and very heavy piece of equipment.
highlights: Baca Funeral Home 1890s Horse-Drawn Hearse & Sleigh
Deming's First Working Traffic Light & Vintage Gas Pump
Mahoney Hardware & The Museum-Founding Washing Machine
Recreated Main Street Shops: Barber, Dentist, Millinery & Post Office
The Deming Headlight Newspaper & Heavy Antique Printing Press

title: Geodes Display
subtitle: The Geode Kid Collection, Thundereggs & Agates
transcript: The Geode Kid Collection brings together geodes, thundereggs, petrified wood, fossils, and other minerals from across the region — many collected right here in Luna County and the surrounding area. So, what exactly is a geode? Picture a plain, unassuming rock — until you crack it open and find a hollow chamber lined with sparkling crystals. That's a geode: a spherical rock, formed inside sedimentary or volcanic stone, hiding a secret world of minerals inside. Those crystals grow when mineral-rich water seeps into small cavities (called vesicles) within volcanic rock and slowly fills them in. In other cases, a geode forms as older mineral deposits dissolve away, leaving a hollow that groundwater or hot fluids later begin to refill. Either way, the result is one of nature's most satisfying surprises. Some of the best geode hunting grounds nearby sit on private property, off-limits to visitors. But Rockhound State Park, just southeast of Deming, is a happy exception — one of the rare state parks in the country where you're welcome to take home what you find. Rockhounds here regularly turn up beautiful agates, and some get lucky and find thundereggs: solid, crystal-filled spheres that look like geodes but aren't quite the same thing. Many of the thundereggs on display in this museum were collected right here, in the Luna County and Mimbres Valley area. What is a thunderegg, exactly? Picture a round, unassuming nodule — usually about the size of a baseball, though they range from under an inch to more than three feet across — that forms inside layers of rhyolitic volcanic ash. Crack one open and you might find a center of chalcedony, fractured and re-decorated over time with bands of agate, jasper, or opal, sometimes all three at once. Quartz and gypsum crystals often show up too, along with other mineral surprises. From the outside, a thunderegg looks like an ordinary rock. Slice and polish one, though, and it can reveal patterns and colors unique to the very bed it came from — no two are ever quite alike. So how do a geode, a thunderegg, and an agate differ? A geode is defined by its hollow center, often lined with crystals. A thunderegg is a specific kind of formation — some thundereggs do have a hollow center and could technically be called geodes, but not every geode is a thunderegg, since hollows form in plenty of other ways too. And a thunderegg, in turn, is really just one particular form that agate can take. Nature, it turns out, has more than one way to make a masterpiece.
highlights: The Geode Kid Mineral & Fossil Collection
Hollow Sparkling Crystal Geodes
Luna County & Mimbres Valley Thundereggs
Rockhound State Park Legal Collecting Area
Polished Chalcedony, Agate, Jasper & Opal

title: Hispanic Room
subtitle: Deep-Rooted Heritage, Southwest History & Nacio Herb Brown
transcript: The Hispanic Room is one of the most quietly powerful spaces in this museum. To understand why this room exists, you must understand something about this land. Long before Deming was a railroad town – long before the silver spike was driven here in 1881 connecting the southern transcontinental railroad, this was Mexico. Luna County, this valley, these streets we walk today, were once part of a Spanish and then Mexican world. That history didn't disappear when the borders shifted. It stayed woven into the daily life of this community – in the language spoken in homes, in the food on the table, in the faith carried from one generation to the next. That's what you'll find preserved here. This room holds the everyday textures of that Hispanic heritage – the objects, images, and traditions that tell the story of the families who built and sustained this region long before it ever appeared on a railroad map. It's a reminder that Deming's identity was never singular. It was shaped by Mimbres potters a thousand years ago, by Apache and Spanish soldiers at Fort Cummings, by railroad workers from a dozen different backgrounds and running through all of it, a deep and enduring Hispanic presence that predates the town itself. There's a small, almost playful detail in this room that captures something bigger: an old sign reading "Hot Tamales – 10 cents." It's a simple thing. But it's also a doorway. It reminds us that history isn't only found in treaties and railroad ledgers – it's found on street corners, in kitchens, in the small commerce of ordinary life. That sign could have hung outside a home in this very neighborhood, sold by a family whose descendants may still live in Luna County today. The Hispanic community is proud of its heritage. Nacio Herb Brown was born in Deming. He was a composer of songs, movie scores and Broadway theatre from the 1920s through the early 1950s. Some of his popular compositions you may recognize are: Singin' in the Rain, Temptation, and music from the Hopalong Cassidy TV series. The community stepped up to name a park after him. So, as you walk through this room, ask yourself to think of it not as a static exhibit, but as a living thread – one that connects the Mexico this land once was, to the Deming it became, to the community we stand in today. The potter, the artifacts, the photographs – they're not just relics. They're proof that this heritage never left. It simply became part of the foundation everything else was built on.
highlights: Pre-1881 Spanish & Mexican Borderlands Heritage
Everyday Cultural Artifacts & Historic 10¢ Hot Tamales Sign
Nacio Herb Brown (Composer of 'Singin' in the Rain' Born in Deming)
Fort Cummings, Apache & Transcontinental Crossroads
Living Cultural Traditions & Enduring Community Legacy

title: Czechoslovakian Display
subtitle: 1920s Heritage, Czech Farming & The Annual Klobase Festival
transcript: The history of Deming's Czechoslovakian community began in the 1920s. Czech immigrants were fleeing the civil war in their home country. Many were cotton farmers searching for rich farming land as they migrated to America, through Ellis Island and the ports of Galveston, Texas. Several Czech families settled in Deming and began farming. In the fall, the families would gather to celebrate the end of the harvest season by gathering and sharing their heritage foods, which included Klobase. In 1928, the Czech immigrants, who attended Holy Family Catholic church, organized a fundraiser and the first official Klobase Festival started. Traditional Czech food was served to the community under the trees at the Kostelnik Farm and the casings for the Klobase were brought in from Texas. As the event grew, more preparation space was needed and the space moved to the Knights of Columbus building which is now part of the Luna County Sheriff Office. Frankie and Kathy Hervol, who bought the Kostelnik Farm in 1972, donated the land and building back to the church so that the Klobase Festival would have a permanent preparation location to where it started in 1928. The festival is held on the third Sunday of October at Luna County Courthouse Park, serves approximately 2,500 people and the Old Timers group coordinates their yearly reunion with this festival. Today the descendants of the founders of this festival carry on the tradition of the recipes that have been passed down through the generations.
highlights: 1920s Czech Immigration via Ellis Island & Galveston
Cotton Farming Pioneers of Luna County
1928 First Klobase Festival & Kostelnik Farm
Holy Family Church & Hervol Family Dedication
Annual October Courthouse Park Festival (2,500+ Served)

title: Custom House & Historic Outbuildings
subtitle: Border Commerce & Customs
transcript: Thank you for completing the tour! Outside the main armory stands the historic Custom House, managed by the museum. Built during the era when international trade passed between Mexico and New Mexico territory, it preserves office records, customs stamps, and boundary survey equipment that shaped the border region.
highlights: Historic Border Customs Records
19th-Century Boundary Survey Tools
Museum Annex & Courtyard
